a: In the third year of Jehoiakim's rule
t: The third year of Jehoiakim, or the fourth?
p: Daniel says the third year; Jeremiah dates Nebuchadnezzar's first year to Jehoiakim's fourth. Several solutions exist.
b: Jeremiah 25:1 and Jeremiah 46:2 put the year of Carchemish and Nebuchadnezzar's first year in Jehoiakim's fourth year (605 BC). Daniel says third. Four main answers: (1) Different counting. Babylon counted the year a king took the throne as his accession year, and Judah may have counted it as year one; the two systems differ by one (Thiele, Archer, Baldwin). (2) Different events. Nebuchadnezzar swept through Syria-Palestine in 605 and again in 604, when the Babylonian Chronicle says all the kings of Hatti-land brought him tribute; Daniel's "came" could mean either. (3) A slip or a schematic date by a writer far from the events (Collins; Hartman and Di Lella). (4) Both Greek versions (the Old Greek as Swete prints it, and Theodotion) read "third year" here, so the number is old. Second Kings 24:1 says Jehoiakim served Babylon three years and then rebelled; 2 Chronicles 36:6-7 adds that vessels were taken. The site follows the Kings chronology; the fall of Jerusalem is dated 586 BC (some scholars say 587).

t: Shinar: Babylonia, and a name with a history
p: Shinar is the old Hebrew name for the plain of Babylon, and the name of the tower story.
b: Shin'ar is the Bible's name for southern Mesopotamia, probably from Sumer. It is the land of Nimrod's kingdom and of the tower (Genesis 10:10; 11:2). Zechariah puts a house for the woman called Wickedness there (Zechariah 5:11), and Isaiah lists it among the lands where exiles are scattered (Isaiah 11:11). Daniel's first scene therefore opens in the place where, in Israel's memory, humanity first tried to make a name by its own building. The vessels of God's house go to the house of a god of that land. See the chapter 1 page for Claude's theory about Shinar and the plain of Dura ("Claude's theory: Daniel opens in Shinar").
r: Genesis 10:10; Genesis 11:2; Genesis 14:1; Joshua 7:21; Isaiah 11:11; Zechariah 5:11

a: The Lord handed Jehoiakim king of Judah over to him
p: The writer says the Lord, not Babylon's gods, handed the king over. 'The Lord' here is Adonai, not the divine name.
b: Daniel opens with a claim: Nebuchadnezzar won because God gave Jehoiakim into his hand. The Hebrew word for "Lord" is Adonai, not the divine name YHWH. In this book the name YHWH occurs only in Daniel 9; elsewhere God is "God" (Elohim, Aramaic 'elah), "the Most High" or "the God of the heavens", names that sound at home in a foreign court. The same word "gave" returns at 1:9 and 1:17: God is the giver at each step. The prophets said the same of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:6; Jeremiah 25:9).

p: Taking a defeated people's sacred objects to the winner's temple said that the winner's god had won.
b: Ancient armies carried the sacred objects of a conquered people to their own gods' houses; the message was that the victor's god had beaten the loser's. Second Kings 24:13 and 25:13-15, 2 Chronicles 36:7 and Jeremiah 27:16-22 list the vessels taken in the successive attacks. These vessels come back as the center of Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:2-3) and are returned under Cyrus (Ezra 1:7). Daniel says only "some" were taken now, which fits the sources: Kings records the first large removal in 597 BC, 2 Chronicles earlier removals.
r: 2 Kings 24:13; 2 Kings 25:13-15; 2 Chronicles 36:7; Jeremiah 27:16-22; Ezra 1:7; Daniel 5:2

t: Eunuch or court official? And was Daniel one?
p: Hebrew saris can mean a castrated man or any court officer. Whether Daniel became one is a question the text leaves open.
b: The Hebrew saris (plural sarisim) is the same word the site renders "eunuchs" in Esther. In Hebrew it can mean a castrated attendant or simply an officer (Potiphar is called a saris, Genesis 39:1, though he was married). Isaiah told Hezekiah that his sons would "serve as eunuchs in the Babylonian king's palace" (Isaiah 39:7), and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 93b) records a dispute over that word: Rav says Daniel and his friends were literally made eunuchs, while Rabbi Hanina says it means that idolatry was emasculated in their time. The text of Daniel never says it, and the young men are chosen for being "without blemish" and then for training, not for their condition. Whether Daniel was made a eunuch is therefore a reading, not a statement.

a: the writing and the language of the Chaldeans
p: 'Chaldeans' means a people of southern Babylonia, and in Daniel also a class of learned men.
b: The Kasdim were a people of southern Babylonia whose dynasty (Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar, from 626 BC) ruled Babylon; the site calls them "the Chaldeans", as in 2 Kings 25. In Daniel the word also names a class of scholars who read omens and advised the king (2:2, 4, 10; 4:7; 5:7). Critics note that this use is best known from Greek writers (Herodotus, Histories 1.181) and later, and take it as a sign of a later writer; defenders reply that the learned class may have borne the national name earlier than our records show. The "writing and language" would be Akkadian and the old cuneiform lore of omens, medicine and stars, learned in scribal schools. Daniel's Aramaic (2:4) is a different matter: it was the everyday speech of the empire.

t: A Persian word in a Babylonian court?
p: The word for the king's food, patbag, is a Persian loanword. Both sides use it in the dating argument.
b: Patbag (1:5, 8, 13, 15, 16; also 11:26) comes from Old Persian patibaga, "portion" or "food". Critics say a Babylonian court of 605 BC would not have used a Persian word, so the author wrote under Persian or later rule. Defenders say the book was put into its present form after 539 BC by Daniel or his circle, when Persian words were everywhere, or that some Persian terms reached Babylon earlier through the Medes. The Plain says "rich food" because the word implies a choice portion from the royal table. The question belongs to the larger one of Daniel's date; see the opening pages.

t: Three years, and the second year (2:1)
p: Three years of training do not fit easily with 'the second year' of 2:1. Counting rules and other answers.
b: If the young men arrive in Nebuchadnezzar's accession year (605 BC) and train "three years", they would present themselves in his third year, yet Daniel interprets the dream in the second year (2:1). Answers: (1) Ancient counting included parts of years, so three "years" can be one full year and parts of two others, and Babylon did not count the accession year as year one (Archer, Baldwin and others). (2) Chapter 2 begins a separate story, set at another time (Papyrus 967, the oldest Old Greek witness, is reported to read "twelfth year" there; see the variant at 2:1). (3) The author joined older stories without making them fit (Collins). Notice also that in 2:25 Arioch presents Daniel as a stranger, though 1:19 has him already standing before the king.

p: Each Hebrew name has God's name in it. The new names point to Babylon's gods.
b: The four Hebrew names speak of God: Daniel "God is my judge", Hananiah "the LORD has been gracious", Mishael "who is what God is?", Azariah "the LORD has helped". The new names do not; Nebuchadnezzar later says Belteshazzar was named for his god (Daniel 4:8, naming Bel). Belteshazzar is usually explained as Akkadian for "protect his life"; Abednego is widely taken as a scribal change of Abed-nabu, "servant of Nabu"; Shadrach and Meshach are uncertain. Renaming a captive was a mark of ownership, as when Pharaoh renamed Joseph (Genesis 41:45) and Babylon renamed Mattaniah Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). The story keeps calling Daniel by his own name.

t: Why would the king's food defile?
p: The text does not say why. Four main explanations.
b: The verb is ga'al, "stain, defile", not the usual word for ritually unclean. Why the royal table would do it is not stated, and readers have differed. (1) Forbidden meats or meat not drained of blood (Leviticus 11; 17:10-14). (2) Idolatry: food and wine were first offered to the gods, with a libation; Judith refused Holofernes' food (Judith 12:2), Tobit and his group kept apart from Gentile food (Tobit 1:10-11), and Judas Maccabeus' band lived on wild plants to avoid defilement (2 Maccabees 5:27). (3) Obligation: eating from the king's table meant being his dependent. (4) Piety under captivity in general. Wine has no ban in the law, so the third and fourth answers, or a mix of reasons, are often preferred. Josephus tells of priests sent to Rome who ate only figs and nuts, for a like reason (Life 13-14).
r: Leviticus 11:1-8; Judith 12:2; Tobit 1:10-11; 2 Maccabees 5:27; Ezekiel 4:13-14; Hosea 9:3

p: The same pair of ideas comes at Joseph's rise and in the prayers of Ezra and Nehemiah.
b: "Loyal love" is hesed (the site's word for it everywhere) and "compassion" is rachamim, a word from the womb, "tender feeling" (the site's word for it in Lamentations). God moves the heart of an official, as he did for Joseph in the jail (Genesis 39:21) and for Ezra before the king (Ezra 7:28), and as Nehemiah prayed (Nehemiah 1:11). The head of the eunuchs is still afraid for his own neck in 1:10, so grace and fear stand side by side.

p: The Hebrew zo'afim means out of sorts or in a sour mood; 'thin' is a guess.
b: Zo'afim occurs elsewhere for a sullen or dejected face (Genesis 40:6, of Pharaoh's two servants) and for rage (Proverbs 19:12, of a king). Older English had "worse liking" (KJV). Some versions say "thinner" or "haggard", but the word describes mood more than weight. The point is that unhappy-looking young men would make the overseer look bad.

p: Zero'im means food grown from seed: grain, pulse and vegetables. It echoes the plants of Genesis 1:29.
b: Zero'im (here with the article, hazzero'im) comes from the word for seed. It covers anything sown: pulse, grain, vegetables. The Old Greek (as Swete prints it) has "pulse" (ospria); Theodotion has "seeds" (spermata). Daniel's request is like the first human diet in Eden (Genesis 1:29), when God gave every plant that makes seed. Most readers see a simple test of faith, not a plan for health.

p: The result in 1:15 is a sign of God's favor, not a rule about diet.
b: Some use these verses to say that plant food is better than meat. The text does not say that. The narrator gives the result after ten days (1:15) and then credits God, not the diet, for the young men's learning (1:17). The ten-day test is a way of showing that those who refuse the king's table lose nothing. Later Daniel mourns by going without choice food (10:3), which shows the same pious restraint, not a health plan.

a: God gave these four young men
p: God 'gives' at three points in chapter 1, and Daniel's gift with dreams recalls Joseph.
b: The verb "give" (natan) marks the chapter: God gives Jehoiakim to Nebuchadnezzar (1:2), favor to Daniel (1:9) and learning to the four (1:17). Daniel's gift with "visions and dreams" parallels Joseph, who also served a foreign king and said that interpretations belong to God (Genesis 40:8; Genesis 41:16). The links between Joseph, Mordecai and Daniel are what scholars call the "court tale": a Jew at a foreign court wins favor by wisdom and faith.

p: A list of terms for Babylon's experts. The Plain keeps one English word for each.
b: The Plain uses one English word for each term, here and in chapters 2 to 5. Chartummim, "magicians", is an Egyptian loanword (Genesis 41:8; Exodus 7:11); 'ashshafim, "enchanters", is related to the Akkadian ashipu, the exorcist-priest; mekhashshefim (2:2) are "sorcerers" (Exodus 22:18); kasdim are "the Chaldeans" (see 1:4); gazrin (2:27) are "diviners", literally those who decide fates. Chakkimin are "wise men", the general title. In Babylon these experts studied omens, medicine, stars and ritual. Daniel and his friends are counted with them (2:13) but are ten times better.
r: Genesis 41:8; Exodus 7:11; Exodus 22:18; Daniel 2:2; Daniel 2:27; Daniel 5:11

a: the first year of King Cyrus
p: The first year of Cyrus is 539/538 BC. It marks that Daniel outlived the empire; it does not say he died.
b: Cyrus entered Babylon in October 539 BC; his first year as king of Babylon is counted from 538. The line says Daniel stayed at court until the end of the empire that took him. It does not say he died then, since Daniel 10:1 puts a vision in Cyrus' third year. From 605 to 538 would give Daniel some 67 years in Babylon. Cyrus' own record is the Cylinder, which presents him as restoring the gods and sending peoples home.

p: The idiom is unclear: sleep left him, or sleep was upon him. Ancient versions took it as 'left him'.
b: The Hebrew says literally "his sleep happened upon him" (nihyetah 'alav). The Greek versions say "his sleep went from him", the Latin Vulgate "sleep fled from him", and the KJV "his sleep brake from him". A few modern readers take it as "a deep sleep fell on him", but the troubled spirit in the same verse and the king's urgency in 2:2 favor "he could not sleep". The dreams (plural) are a single dream retold in 2:3 and 2:31-35.

t: The book changes language in mid-sentence
p: Here the text stops being Hebrew and becomes Aramaic. It stays Aramaic to the end of chapter 7.
b: The Hebrew word aramit, "in Aramaic", marks the switch inside the verse; the speech that follows is in Aramaic and so is everything to 7:28. Hebrew returns at 8:1. In the Qumran copy 1QDan-a (1Q71) the words "O king, live forever" are visible straight after "to the king" (the word aramit itself is restored there, so the scroll shows the Aramaic running on but does not show the marker). Why? (1) The writer reports the Chaldeans' speech in their language and goes on in it. (2) The Aramaic chapters (2-7) were an older collection that a later writer framed with Hebrew chapters 1 and 8-12 (Collins and many others). (3) Chapters 2-7 form a chiasm: four kingdoms (2) and (7), the furnace (3) and the den (6), the two proud kings (4) and (5) (Lenglet, 1972); the Aramaic marks that unit. (4) Torrey suggested that chapters 1-7 were first Aramaic. (5) Aramaic was the language of Jews scattered through the empire, Hebrew of the holy city and the future. Both Greek versions render the word "in Syriac" (Syristi), the Greek name for Aramaic. No view has won; the word aramit might even be a scribe's note, as in Ezra 4:7. See the opening pages and the topic on Aramaic.

p: The KJV took the king to say the dream had slipped his mind. Most commentators now read 'my word is firm'.
b: The Aramaic milta minni 'azda has an odd word, 'azda. The Greek (both the Old Greek and Theodotion) read "the word has gone from me", the Vulgate "the word has left me", and so the KJV: "The thing is gone from me", as if the king had forgotten the dream. Many modern commentators instead take 'azda as a Persian word meaning "known, certain" and read "my decision is fixed". Two things favor this: the rest of the scene has the king remember his dream perfectly well (2:31-35 describes it in detail), and 2:8 repeats the phrase after "you see that" (he is not hiding forgetfulness but a final decision). The oldest copy, 1QDan-a (1Q71), has 'azda visible, as the Masoretic Text does, so the odd word is old. Persian loanwords are part of the dating debate.

a: hacked apart, and your houses will be made a dunghill
p: Dismemberment and turning a house into a refuse heap are royal threats found again in Ezra and Daniel 3:29.
b: "Hacked apart" is hadamin, limbs cut off; "dunghill" is nevali, a refuse heap or latrine. The same pair of threats appears in Daniel 3:29, and the second in the decree of Darius in Ezra 6:11. Jehu did the same to Baal's temple (2 Kings 10:27, "toilets"). Such threats show how a king's word could ruin a family's whole property as well as its life.

p: The Chaldeans speak as polytheists. The Plain keeps 'the gods' where they speak and 'God' where Daniel does.
b: 'Elahin is a plural, "gods". The site's rule: "the gods" when a pagan speaks (here and 3:25; also 4:8-9, 18; 5:11, 14, where the Aramaic can also be read "a holy god"), and "God" for Israel's God, in the singular ('elah, as in 2:20). The Chaldeans' point is true on their own terms: no human power can read a king's dream unaided. Daniel will say in 2:28 that there is such a God, and in heaven. The Old Greek (as Swete prints it) has "an angel" here, not "gods"; Theodotion has "gods".

p: The title 'chief of the executioners' also belongs to Potiphar and to Nebuzaradan.
b: The title rav tabbachaya is the Aramaic form of sar hatabbachim, literally "chief of the butchers", the commander of the royal guard and executioner (Genesis 37:36 for Potiphar; 2 Kings 25:8 for Nebuzaradan, who burned Jerusalem). The name Arioch is old; a man of that name is a king in Genesis 14:1, and it appears in Mari texts of the 1700s BC, as commentators note. It is an archaic touch, but not a sign of the sixth century in itself.

p: This title belongs to the Persian-period Jews: Ezra, Nehemiah, Elephantine and Daniel.
b: The title 'elah shemayya appears in Daniel 2:18-19, 37, 44; in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 1:2; 5:11-12; 6:9-10; 7:12, 21, 23; Nehemiah 1:4-5; 2:4, 20); and in the Aramaic letters of the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt (about 407 BC), which call YHW "the God of the heavens". It also occurs in Genesis 24:3, 7, Jonah 1:9 and Psalm 136:26. The word "heaven" is a plural form in Aramaic and Hebrew; the site's Ezra and Nehemiah say "the God of the heavens", and so does Daniel's Plain here, for the same words. The singular "a God in heaven" at 2:28 is a different Aramaic form (bishmayya). The title suits a God addressed by Jews to people of other nations: he is not tied to one temple, since the temple lies in ruins.
r: Ezra 1:2; Ezra 5:11; Nehemiah 1:4; Nehemiah 2:4; Jonah 1:9; Psalm 136:26; Genesis 24:7

p: Raz, 'secret', is a Persian word that both Greek versions render with mysterion, the word Paul later used.
b: Raz (2:18-19, 27-30, 47; 4:9) is borrowed from Persian and means a hidden thing known only to a few, here a king's dream and what it means. Both Greek versions of Daniel render it mysterion ("mystery"). Paul's "mystery" (Romans 16:25-26; 1 Corinthians 2:7; Ephesians 3:3-9; Colossians 1:26-27) is the same word, and Revelation 1:20 calls the stars and lampstands a "mystery". In Daniel, the word always has the sense that God alone uncovers a hidden plan.
r: Romans 16:25; 1 Corinthians 2:7; Ephesians 3:3; Colossians 1:26; Revelation 1:20; Daniel 4:9

a: Let the name of God be blessed
p: The hymn praises God's wisdom and power, and shares phrases with Job and the Psalms.
b: This is the first of the prayers in Daniel and the first poetry in the Aramaic section. It thanks God for knowing and for ruling history. It shares ideas with Job 12:13 and 12:22 (wisdom and power are God's; he uncovers deep things from darkness) and with Psalm 113:2 (the name blessed forever). Notice that Daniel speaks of what God has just given "us" (2:23), the four friends together, and that he thanks God before he has told the king anything.

a: changes the periods and the appointed times
t: God removes and sets up kings
p: A statement of God's control over history. It sets the theme for chapters 2 to 7.
b: "Periods" and "appointed times" are 'iddanayya and zimnayya, the world's times and the appointed days. The line about kings is the book's theme in a sentence: God removes kings and sets them up, as Nebuchadnezzar will learn (4:17, 25, 32) and Belshazzar too (5:21). Jeremiah had said the same about Babylon's rise (Jeremiah 27:5-7) and Isaiah about Persian and other rulers (Isaiah 40:23-24; 45:1-4). A king hears this hymn as a threat as well as a comfort.

p: Not always the end of the world: it can mean the later part of a story. Revelation takes the line over.
b: The Aramaic be'achrit yomayya matches the Hebrew be'acharit hayyamim (Genesis 49:1; Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). In the prophets it often means "in the time to come" and sometimes the final age. Here Daniel says the dream shows what will come after the king's own day; the stone brings in God's kingdom (2:44), so the sense moves toward the end. Theodotion's Greek, "what must happen in the last days", is the phrase that Revelation uses over and over (Revelation 1:1, 19; 4:1; 22:6). Whether the "last days" are Hellenistic times, the first coming of Christ, or a final age depends on the reading of the kingdoms; see 2:39.
r: Genesis 49:1; Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Deuteronomy 4:30; Revelation 1:1; Revelation 1:19; Revelation 4:1

p: The idea of a series of metals as a series of ages, and of four empires, is older than Daniel in Greek and other sources.
b: The Aramaic tselem is the word for "image" in Genesis 1:26, here a standing figure. The decline from gold to iron recalls Hesiod's ages (Works and Days 109-201: gold, silver, bronze, a heroic age, iron), and four-empire lists appear in Greek and Roman writers (Aemilius Sura in Velleius Paterculus 1.6.6) and in the Sibylline Oracles (book 4). Scholars differ on whether Daniel borrowed the scheme or the schemes share an older Near Eastern root (Flusser; Collins). Summary: a real, shared pattern; Daniel gives it a Jewish twist, since the empires end when God, not the next empire, intervenes. The statue image also echoes the Bible's ridicule of man-made gods (Isaiah 44:9-20).

p: The stone is not made by any human power. The phrase returns in the New Testament about the temple and about circumcision.
b: The Aramaic is simply "not by hands" (di la bidayin). Theodotion's Greek, aneu cheiron, "without hands", is close to the New Testament's acheiropoietos, "not made by hands". Mark 14:58 reports the charge that Jesus said he would build another temple "not made with hands"; Hebrews 9:11, 24 and 2 Corinthians 5:1 contrast what is made by hands with what God makes; Colossians 2:11 uses it of circumcision. In Daniel the phrase says that God's kingdom does not arise out of a human empire. Both Greek versions also add "from a mountain" here (see the variant), taking the word from 2:45.
r: Mark 14:58; Hebrews 9:11; 2 Corinthians 5:1; Colossians 2:11; Acts 7:48; Daniel 8:25

a: You are the head of gold
p: Jeremiah had said God gave all these lands to Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel says the same, and sets a limit to it.
b: The "head of gold" is Nebuchadnezzar and, many take it, his dynasty. Jeremiah spoke the same way: God gave the lands, and even the animals, to Nebuchadnezzar his servant (Jeremiah 27:5-7). The king hears praise, since gold is the best metal, and a warning, since the metal that comes next is lower, and the whole figure will be smashed. The "all the earth" is the world as Daniel's readers knew it.

a: another kingdom will rise, lower than yours
p: Only the head, Babylon, is named. Jews and Christians have read the other three in different ways.
b: Daniel names the first kingdom (2:38). The rest are left to the reader. Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece is the view of the critical majority (Collins and many others): a Median kingdom (Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11, 28; Darius the Mede, Daniel 5:31) then Persia; the iron kingdom is Alexander's successors and the feet the Ptolemies and Seleucids. Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome is the main line of the early church (Hippolytus, Jerome) and Calvin; the rabbis too often make the fourth "Edom", meaning Rome (Genesis Rabbah 2:4; Leviticus Rabbah 13:5). Some futurists keep Rome as the fourth and look for its last form (Walvoord). Josephus declined to explain the stone (Antiquities 10.210). The identification matters, since it fixes when the stone is thought to strike. The full comparison is on the topic page, and chapter 7 returns to it.
r: Daniel 7:3; Daniel 7:17; Daniel 8:20; Daniel 11:2; Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11

a: The fourth kingdom will be hard as iron
p: On one reading the iron is Alexander and the Greek kings; on another, Rome.
b: The iron is a power that breaks and grinds everything. In the Greek reading it describes Alexander's conquests and the kingdoms of the Seleucids and Ptolemies; Daniel 7:7 describes a fourth beast with iron teeth, and Daniel 11 narrates the Hellenistic kings. In the Roman reading (Hippolytus, Jerome and most Christian commentators; the rabbis who say Edom) it fits Rome's legions. Neither reading is the plain sense of the words alone; each fits the detail of the feet differently. See 2:39 and the topic page.

a: The toes of the feet were part iron and part clay
t: Ten toes? The text does not count
p: A common idea says the toes are ten kings. The chapter gives no number.
b: It is often said that the ten toes are ten kings, matching the ten horns of Daniel 7:7, 24. In chapter 2 the toes are never counted; the text speaks of "the feet and the toes" as part of one divided kingdom (2:41). A link to the ten horns may be real, but chapter 2 does not say it. The English "toes" translates a plural word, and the plural alone does not give ten.

p: The Aramaic says they will be mixed with 'the seed of humankind'. It may mean marriage alliances.
b: "Seed of mankind" (zera' 'enasha) is usually taken as a reference to marriages between ruling families. In the Hellenistic reading, this is the Seleucid and Ptolemaic marriages that Daniel 11:6 and 11:17 describe, which did not bind the two kingdoms together. Others read a mixture of Roman and non-Roman peoples, or of the final empire with other nations. The phrase "will not stick" is the point: the mixture is weak.

a: a kingdom that will never be ruined
t: The stone and the kingdom of God
p: All agree the stone is God's doing. Readers disagree on when it arrives and who it is.
b: Early Christian writers took the stone to be Christ and the kingdom to be his: Irenaeus even reads "not by hands" of the virgin birth (Against Heresies 3.21.7); Hippolytus, Jerome and Calvin read the kingdom as begun in Christ and growing in the church. Futurist readers place the blow at the second coming, after a last form of the fourth kingdom (Walvoord). Critical scholars see God's own reign replacing the Hellenistic kingdoms, given in the vision of chapter 7 to "the people of the holy ones of the Most High" (Daniel 7:27). Jewish readers have long seen the end of the nations' rule and the day of the Messiah. Josephus said he was writing history and would not explain the stone (Antiquities 10.210). Jesus' saying about the stone that crushes (Matthew 21:44) is often linked to this verse.
orig: מַלְכוּ דִּי לְעָלְמִין לָא תִתְחַבַּל (malku di le'olmin la titchabbal)

p: The king bows and orders offerings. The text does not say Daniel agrees or refuses.
b: Nebuchadnezzar's act looks like worship (the verb segid is the one used of the golden statue in chapter 3), and offerings of grain and incense belong to gods. The narrator says nothing about Daniel's answer. Some readers think Daniel declined and that the story passes over it; others point to the king's own next words, which give the glory to Daniel's God (2:47), and others to Peter's refusal of Cornelius' bow (Acts 10:25-26). Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes at Lystra (Acts 14:11-15), and an angel refused worship in Revelation 19:10. The Greek versions also differ: the Old Greek (as Swete prints it) has offerings and libations ordered; Theodotion has a gift and sweet smells. In the story's logic the king is learning, not yet converted.

a: God of gods and the lord of kings
t: A king's confession, not yet a conversion
p: Foreign kings praise Daniel's God again in 3:28, 4:34 and 6:26. The pattern is repeated and does not last.
b: "God of gods and Lord of lords" is a title from Deuteronomy 10:17 and Psalm 136:2-3. The pagan king's confession is a pattern in the Aramaic chapters: Nebuchadnezzar again after the furnace (3:28-29) and after his madness (4:34-37), and Darius after the lions (6:25-27). Each time he praises God and issues orders; yet Nebuchadnezzar builds a golden statue in the very next chapter. The stories seem to say that a king can confess God's power without worshiping him alone.

a: chief of the prefects over all the wise men of Babylon
p: A Jew raised to rule beside a foreign king: Joseph, Daniel, Mordecai and Nehemiah.
b: Joseph was made ruler of Egypt after interpreting a king's dream (Genesis 41:40-43), Mordecai second to the king (Esther 10:3), and Daniel ruler of the province of Babylon and chief of the prefects over the wise men. Scholars treat these as the "court tale" pattern (Humphreys; Collins): a Jew who is wise and loyal both to the king and to God, in danger and then raised. Note the irony: Daniel is set over the very men who failed and whom he saved from death (2:24).

a: sixty cubits tall and six cubits across
t: A statue ten times as tall as wide
p: About 90 feet by 9 feet. The odd proportions suggest a pedestal or an obelisk with a figure on top, or a symbolic size.
b: A cubit is about 18 inches (45 cm), so the statue is about 90 feet (27 m) high and 9 feet (2.7 m) wide: a ratio of ten to one, far thinner than a human body. Suggestions: the figure stood on a tall base; it was a pillar or obelisk; the numbers are symbolic. "Of gold" probably means gilded wood or clay, as in Isaiah 40:19. It is not said whom the statue shows; it may be Nebuchadnezzar, a god such as Nabu or Marduk, or the empire itself. The Old Greek and Theodotion both put it in the king's "eighteenth year" (see the variant), the year when Jerusalem's last deportation was under way (Jeremiah 52:29).

p: Many places in Babylonia were called Dura, 'wall' or 'fortress'. The site is unknown.
b: The Akkadian duru means "wall" or "fortress", and many sites in Mesopotamia were called Dura. No excavation has fixed this plain, "in the province of Babylon". The word translated "plain" is the one in Genesis 11:2, where people settled on a plain in Shinar and began the tower. See the chapter 1 page for Claude's theory that links the two scenes. Theodotion spells the name Deeira; the Old Greek (as Swete prints it) renders it by sense, "the plain of the enclosure" (pedion tou peribolou), which fits the meaning "wall".

a: the satraps, the prefects, the governors, the advisers, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates
p: Eight titles, mostly Persian words. The list is repeated word for word, a mark of the storytelling.
b: The list of eight offices (3:2 and again in 3:3) is repeated word for word, as the list of instruments is. Most of the titles are Persian loanwords (satrap, "adviser", "treasurer", "judge"); two, "prefect" and "governor", are Akkadian; the meaning of "magistrates" is uncertain. The exact sense of each title is not known and translations differ. The Persian words are part of the dating argument: critics say they point to Persian times or later, and defenders say a book written down or revised under the Persians would use the Persian court's words. The Plain keeps the titles in a fixed order.

p: A phrase that recurs six times in Daniel and returns in Revelation. Here it recalls Babel.
b: The triple phrase 'amemayya, 'umayya, lishanayya comes again at 3:7, 3:29, 4:1, 5:19, 6:25 and 7:14: the whole empire, and at last all peoples serving the one like a son of man. Here the herald calls every language to one act of worship at one signal; at Babel (Genesis 11:1-9) a single language went to one building and God scattered it. Revelation takes the phrase for those who worship the Lamb and for those who worship the beast (Revelation 7:9; 13:7; 17:15).
r: Genesis 11:1; Daniel 3:7; Daniel 3:29; Daniel 6:25; Daniel 7:14; Revelation 7:9; Revelation 13:7

a: the horn, the flute, the zither, the triangle-lyre, the harp, the pipes
p: Three of the six instrument names are Greek words. They are used in the date debate by both sides.
b: The six names are qarna (horn), mashroqita (flute or pipe), qatros (written qitaros; zither), sabbeka (triangle-lyre), pesanterin (harp) and sumponya (pipes). Three come from Greek (kithara, psalterion, symphonia); sabbeka is the source of Greek sambyke, which Strabo calls a barbarian word. Critics say Greek music words in a Babylonian court of 600 BC are unlikely and point to Hellenistic times; some add that symphonia is not clearly an instrument name in Greek before the second century BC. Defenders (Kitchen, Millard and others) answer that Greek mercenaries and craftsmen were in Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar's day and that foreign instruments often keep their foreign names. The list is repeated in 3:5, 7, 10, 15; the form with six instruments is full, and 3:7 leaves out the last. Translations differ on the instruments.

p: Babylon is said to have burned people. Jeremiah mentions two men roasted in fire by the king.
b: Jeremiah 29:22 says that the king of Babylon roasted two Judean exiles, Ahab and Zedekiah, in the fire. The "furnace" ('attun) is a kiln or smelter, probably with an opening at the top for loading and one at the side. Ancient Near Eastern law and letters speak of death by fire for some crimes. In the story, the fire punishes the one who will not worship; in the next verses it harms only the king's own men (3:22).

p: The Aramaic idiom means to accuse maliciously. It is the first time the book says 'Jews' (yehudaye).
b: The idiom is "they ate their pieces" ('akalu qartsehon), found also in Akkadian: to tear someone to shreds with accusations. The accusers are "Chaldean men", the learned class (1:4), perhaps jealous of the Jews' promotion (2:49). The word "Jews" (yehudayye) is the Aramaic form; in the Hebrew chapter 1 the young men are "Israelites" and "men of Judah". Note that the charge is not religious in the first telling but political: the three do not give the king a thought (3:12). The wording of the accusation is the first time that Jews in exile are blamed for refusing the state's worship, a pattern found again in Esther 3:8 and in Daniel 6.

p: The Aramaic tsada occurs only here. 'Is it true?' (KJV) and 'Is it on purpose?' are both used.
b: Tsada occurs only here. The KJV has "Is it true?" (taking it from Hebrew tsadah, truth); other readings are "is it on purpose?" (the sense of a related word in Akkadian) or "is it intentional?". The Old Greek (as Swete prints it) has "Why, Shadrach ...?" (dia ti); Theodotion has "Is it true?" (ei alethos), the KJV's sense. The king gives them the chance to say it was a mistake before he repeats the order (3:15).

a: Which god is there that can save you from my hands
p: Other kings have said the same: Pharaoh, Sennacherib's officer.
b: The king's challenge matches earlier boasts: Pharaoh ("Who is the LORD?", Exodus 5:2) and the Assyrian field commander, who asked which god had saved any land from Assyria (2 Kings 18:33-35; Isaiah 36:18-20). In each case the claim is answered by deliverance. The story asks readers who are subject to foreign rulers whether any god can save them.

p: The Aramaic hen ithay is unclear. The Greek takes it as 'there is a God'.
b: The words hen ithay can mean "if there is" or "if it is so" or "if (it comes to that)". The KJV: "If it be so, our God...is able". Theodotion's Greek removes the "if": "For there is a God whom we serve, able to deliver us", and the Old Greek (as Swete prints it): "There is one God in heaven, our Lord, whom we fear". On the Aramaic reading the three answer the king's challenge: if the sentence is carried out, their God is able to save them, and will; the next verse says what happens if he does not. The Plain keeps a conditional ("if it comes to that") and splits the sentence.

p: A famous line of faith. The three do not know how it will end, and say so.
b: The Aramaic is simply "and if not" (vehen la). The three say they will not serve the king's gods whether or not God rescues them, and that is the point of the story: faith that does not depend on the outcome. The tradition took them as martyr models. 1 Maccabees 2:59-60, written about 100 BC, lists Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael among the faithful who were saved. First Clement 45:6-7 (about AD 96) names them with Daniel. In 4 Maccabees (16:21) they are examples for a mother and seven sons who die. The Talmud (Pesachim 53b) treats them as examples of giving one's life to sanctify God's name. Some Christians read the line as the pattern of the martyrs; Jewish teachers see in it kiddush hashem, "sanctifying the Name".

a: their cloaks, their trousers, their caps
t: Clothing words that no one is sure of
p: Three of the four garment names are rare. 'Trousers' and 'caps' are best guesses.
b: The garment terms (sarbal, patish, karbela) are rare and their meanings are guesses from other languages: "cloaks" or "tunics", "trousers" or "hose", "caps" or "turbans". The Old Greek (as Swete prints it) has "shoes" (hypodemata) and "tiaras"; Theodotion has sarabara (a loanword, "trousers"), "tiaras" and "leggings" (periknemisi). The detail is for the story: even clothes that burn easily were not burned (3:27).

a: Then King Nebuchadnezzar was startled and rose quickly.
t: Between verses 23 and 24 in the Greek Bible
p: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles have a long insertion here: the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three.
b: In the Greek Daniel (both the Old Greek and Theodotion) 67 verses come between 3:23 and 3:24, numbered 3:24-90 there; Catholic Bibles print them as Daniel 3:24-90. The Prayer of Azariah (3:26-45 Greek) confesses the nation's sin and asks for rescue; the Song of the Three (3:52-90, the "Benedicite") calls on the creation to bless the Lord. In church use the Song is a Sunday morning canticle in the Roman Catholic Liturgy of the Hours and in the Anglican Book of Common Prayer, and the Orthodox sing it as Odes 7 and 8 of the Matins canon. Protestant Bibles do not include it. See the variant at 3:23 and the book's opening pages on Where Christians differ.

p: Not 'the Son of God' as in the KJV. A pagan king is speaking.
b: The Aramaic bar-'elahin has no article and a plural "gods". Nebuchadnezzar, a polytheist, uses a Semitic idiom for a divine being (compare "sons of God" in Genesis 6:2 and Job 1:6). The KJV's "the Son of God" reads the New Testament title back into a pagan's mouth; Theodotion's Greek ("like a son of God") already narrows it, and the Old Greek has "like an angel of God". The king himself calls the figure "his angel" in 3:28. Christian readers from the early church have often seen the Son of God before his birth (Hippolytus, in a commentary excerpt preserved in the catenae; its authorship is debated); others, Calvin among them, stress that the king could not have meant that and the figure is an angel. Jewish readers speak of angels. In the Talmud (Pesachim 118a) the angel in charge of hail offers to go down and cool the furnace; Gabriel, the angel of fire, objects that water putting out fire would not show God's strength, and offers to cool it from within. The passage does not identify the fourth figure. Two named holders of the Christian reading are given here; other early writers could be added. Hebrews 11:34 says some "quenched the power of fire". The text does not say.

p: A name for God that foreigners also use. It comes again in 4:2, 17, 25, 32, 34 and 7:18-27.
b: "The Most High" is 'illaya in Aramaic and 'Elyon in Hebrew. It is the title with which Melchizedek blesses Abram (Genesis 14:18-22) and which the nations can say without using Israel's name. In Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar learns it in chapter 4 and "the holy ones of the Most High" receive the kingdom in chapter 7. In the Greek the title is hypsistos, the one used of Jesus' Father in Luke 1:32, 35.

p: Compare the angel who shuts the lions' mouths and the angel of the Lord who guards the faithful.
b: The king concludes that the fourth figure was God's angel (mal'ak). In the lions' den Daniel says the same thing (6:22). The idea that God's angel guards and delivers the faithful runs through the psalms and Exodus (Psalm 34:7; Exodus 14:19; 23:20). The Greek Prayer of Azariah (verse 49 in Theodotion's numbering) names the angel of the Lord who came down into the furnace and drove out the flame.

a: prosper in the province of Babylon
t: A numbering break: English 3:30 ends the chapter
p: The Aramaic chapter runs to verse 33; English 4:1-3 is Aramaic 3:31-33.
b: The Hebrew and Aramaic text of Daniel 3 has 33 verses. What English Bibles number 4:1-3 (Nebuchadnezzar's letter beginning "to all peoples, nations and languages") is 3:31-33 in the Aramaic, and English 4:4-37 is Aramaic 4:1-34. This site uses the English numbers everywhere. The Greek text, with its insertion, numbers the furnace chapter to 100 verses. The next part picks up at 4:1.
